catalog_quote: In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). The ultima can have a somewhat more complex structure and a greater variety of phonological content than other syllables. ... In such words initiation of stress (accent) on the ultima vowel is usually perceptible: (C)V1.ˈV1(C). [sec. 4.1.7, p.53] V̆1hV1ː /tăhas/ > [tă.ˈhaʂ] ‘ironwood’ (Bukar-Sadung and Sembaan dialects); [tă.ˈhas] (Rara) (33) [fn.79, p.94] Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached. [Part III sec. 6.2.4, p.292] ... even though an accentual difference is not evident in the contemporary Land Dayak languages. They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position. [Rensch 2008, sec. 2, p.85] Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had
sweep_summary: trin1271 (Tringgus-Sembaan Bidayuh) is not in the catalog. Both title hits are the same work by Calvin Rensch, 'Rhythm in Bidayuh' (2006 10-ICAL web paper; 2008 SPLC 19: 84-91), both already held by the project with text layers (downloaded from SIL and the Internet Archive in the biat1246 search; symlinked into trin1271 and logged). Read in full: the single synchronic stress statement is 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation' (2008 p.85 / 2006 p.2), stated for all four Bidayuh clusters and illustrated with Tringgus Bireng data; the rest of the paper is vowel length and the full/reduced penult contrast (Highland dialects have the full set), plus a diachronic claim that the penult contrast reflects PAN final vs penultimate accent. The 2-page abstract has no placement sentence. The 2012 SIL monograph held by the project (corpus includes Sembaan-Tringgus wordlists) says the same thing more fully (Part II 4.1.2 p.47; fn.79 p.94; Part III 6.2.4 p.292). Nothing left to acquire from these items; the only unread Tringgus-specific sources noted in our earlier reading (Kroeger 1996 'Dialects of Biatah', print; Rahim Aman 2008, UKM print; Google Books snippets only) are wordlist/comparative works, not stress descriptions. all claims come from files opened held by the project and the Glottolog reference records saved in

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable (ultima) of the word/stem in all Bidayuh dialects studied, which include the Sembaan-group dialects Sembaan, Tringgus Raya and Tringgus Bireng; stated for citation forms and most evident utterance-finally. Rensch 2006 'Rhythm in Bidayuh' p.2 restates it ('Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation') and illustrates directly with Tringgus Bireng forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Enclitics attract the stress (fn.79: 'a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached'). Tringgus Raya lacks the ultima vowel-length contrast found in other dialects (Part III sec. 2.1 note; Rensch 2006 p.3), which does not affect stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly hedged to citation forms / words in isolation ('at least in citation forms', 'and perhaps in context'); Part III adds 'especially evident in utterance-final position'. Statement is pan-Bidayuh, not a Tringgus-Sembaan-specific description, but the Sembaan-group wordlists (Sembaan, Tringgus Raya, Tringgus Bireng, collected 2001) are part of the corpus the statement rests on and a Sembaan form is transcribed with ultima stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is made for 'Bidayuh' as a whole (all ~25 dialects in the Rensch corpus), not for Tringgus-Sembaan alone; the corpus explicitly includes the Sembaan-group dialects Sembaan (loc. 20), Tringgus Raya and Tringgus Bireng (loc. 21), i.e. exactly Glottolog trin1271 / ISO trx ('Bidayuh, Tringgus-Sembaan', renamed via CR 2007-244 by the same author). Rensch 2006 groups them as the 'Highland' cluster (Tringgus-Sembaan-Upper Padawan). The same book is already the the deciding source held by the project for biat1246 and rara1235.

new_statements.reading: Fixed final (ultima) word stress on the disyllabic stem, stated for Bidayuh as a whole with the hedge 'at least in isolation', and exemplified first with Tringgus Bireng (Highland cluster = Tringgus-Sembaan-Upper Padawan) forms; Glottolog codes the article to trx. Corroborated by the same author team's monograph already held by the project (Rensch, Rensch, Noeb & Ridu 2012, The Bidayuh Language, SIL e-Books 33, whose 2001 wordlist corpus includes Sembaan-Tringgus): Part II sec. 4.1.2 printed p.47 'In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress--at least in citation forms'; fn.79 printed p.94 'Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement'; Part III sec. 6.2.4 printed p.292 contemporary Land Dayak languages 'consistently accent the final syllable of the stem'. No Tringgus/Sembaan-specific deviation from final stress is stated in any of these; Tringgus Raya is singled out only for lacking the ultima length contrast. Coding for a catalog entry: fixed final stress (with citation-form hedge), based on a language-cluster statement not a Tringgus-only phonology.

sources.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. In both the ultima and the penult there are differences of vowel duration that create contrasting rhythm patterns. The longer (L) and shorter (S) vowels in both ultima and penult occur in all four possible combinations: S-S, L-S, S-L, L-L. sources.note: Published version of the 2006 10-ICAL paper, same wording. One synchronic sentence: word stress is on the ultima (final syllable) of the disyllabic stem, 'at least in isolation'; the sentence is immediately illustrated with Tringgus Bireng (Highland cluster = Tringgus-Sembaan-Upper Padawan) examples, and Tringgus Raya / Sembaan forms recur throughout. The paper's real topic is vowel length in the ultima and the full/reduced penult-vowel contrast (Highland dialects have the complete full/reduced set, Pattern A; Tringgus Raya lacks the ultima length contrast).
